summary: Describes how IANA registers Private Enterprise Numbers, how to request a new one, and how to modify an existing one. It also gives a brief overview of what PENs are used for.

eli5.summary: A company can get its own special number from a central office so its names never clash with anyone else's. This tells you how to ask.

questions: how to register a private enterprise number
how to get an iana enterprise number
subtitle: How to get and manage a Private Enterprise Number for your organization.

tldr.problem: Organizations need unique identifiers to use in protocols and systems, especially when identifying extensions or products that use ASN.1 object identifiers (OIDs), and these identifiers must not conflict with those of other organizations.
tldr.mechanism: IANA allocates Private Enterprise Numbers, which are OIDs starting with the prefix 1.3.6.1.4.1, on a first-come first-served basis. Organizations request a PEN by providing their name and a public contact, then use their assigned number as the root for creating sub-OIDs for their own purposes.
tldr.outcome: Each organization gets a unique identifier space they can subdivide as needed, enabling interoperable use of proprietary extensions and features in standard protocols and configurations.

today: RFC 9371 is an Informational document that documents how IANA registers Private Enterprise Numbers. The PEN registry remains active and open for new assignments at https://www.iana.org/assignments/enterprise-numbers.

sections.title: What are PENs
sections.content:
Private Enterprise Numbers (PENs) are identifiers that can be used wherever an ASN.1 object identifier (OID) can be used. Originally developed so that organizations could identify themselves in Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) Management Information Base (MIB) configurations, PENs have become useful in any application or configuration language that needs OIDs to identify organizations.

The IANA Functions Operator manages the PEN registry. All PENs start with the OID prefix 1.3.6.1.4.1 (representing iso.org.dod.internet.private.enterprise). A complete PEN looks like 1.3.6.1.4.1.32473, and the organization can then create sub-OIDs such as 1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.7 for their own purposes.
sections.eli5: A PEN is like a company code number that identifies the organization in computer systems. It starts with a standard prefix that everyone shares, then adds a unique number for each company.

sections.title: Uses of PENs
sections.content:
Once assigned a PEN, an organization can use it by itself to represent the organization, or as the root for creating other OIDs associated with the organization. For example, an organization might use 1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.7 to identify a proprietary protocol extension and 1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.12.3 to identify a set of algorithms it supports.

PENs are frequently used in IETF protocols to provide unique identifiers. SNMP MIB configuration files use PENs to identify the origin of values. Protocols that use PENs as identifiers for extension mechanisms include RADIUS, Diameter, Syslog, RSVP, and vCard. Critically, IANA and the IETF cannot control how an assignee uses its PEN—the whole point of "private" in the name is that the assignee has full freedom.
sections.eli5: Once a company has a PEN, it can use the number itself, or use sub-numbers under it. For example, a networking protocol might let a company announce its own extensions using its PEN, which tells everyone that the extensions come from that company.

sections.title: Requesting and Managing PENs
sections.content:
PENs are assigned by IANA using the "First Come First Served" registration policy, with values assigned sequentially. Organizations request a PEN by providing the name of the assignee, the name of a public contact who can answer questions about the assignment, and contact information for verifying change requests. The contact's name and email will be listed in the public registry.

An organization may request multiple PENs, but obtaining one PEN and making internal sub-assignments is typically more appropriate. IANA may refuse to process abusive requests. Organizations can modify any information in their registration, including the assignee name, by providing authorization from a representative of the assignee. When a PEN is deleted (a rare occurrence), all identifying information is removed and the value is marked as "returned." Returned values will not be reassigned until all unassigned values have been exhausted.
sections.eli5: To get a PEN, you tell IANA who you are and who to contact about it. IANA assigns numbers in order. If you need to change your information later, you can ask, and IANA will check that you are the owner. If you want to return a PEN, IANA will mark it as used, but won't give it to someone else for a long time.

sections.title: Registry Constraints and Special Values
sections.content:
The range of PEN values after the prefix is 0 to 2^32-1 (4,294,967,295). The values 0 and 4,294,967,295 are reserved and cannot be assigned. While the original PEN definition had no upper bound, an upper bound now exists because some IETF protocols (such as Diameter) limit the PEN value to 2^32-1.

The PEN number 32473 is reserved for use as an example in documentation, as specified in RFC 5612. Values in the registry that have unclear ownership are marked "Reserved." These values will not be reassigned to a new company or individual without consulting the IESG.
sections.eli5: PENs can be any number from 1 to about 4 billion. Some special numbers are kept for examples or for cases where no one remembers who should own them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Registering PENs does not introduce significant security considerations for the registration process itself. However, there is an important limitation: there is no cryptographic binding between a registrant in the PEN registry and the PEN(s) assigned to them. Therefore, entries in the PEN registry cannot be used to validate ownership of a PEN in use. For example, if the PEN 1.3.6.1.4.1.32473 appears in a protocol message indicating the owner of some data, there is no way to securely correlate that use with the name and contact listed in the registry. Users who need to verify ownership of a PEN must rely on other out-of-band mechanisms.
sections.eli5: The registry tells you what company owns each number, but it does not prove ownership if someone uses the number. If you see a number in a message, you cannot be sure just from the registry that the message really came from the owner.
